title: AI at work: jobs that change
essentialQuestion: How might AI change people's jobs, and who gains or loses?
learningGoal: Use examples from history and a 2025 study to explain how new technology changes the tasks in jobs, and why the change is uneven.

warmUp.question: A new machine can do part of a worker's job. What do you think happens to the worker?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: For each worker, which tasks changed? Who gained, and who lost?

cards.title: Three workers in the town of Millbrook

cases.name: Clerks at the water office
cases.body: Ines and two other clerks typed up customer forms. Now an AI tool reads most forms and fills in the details. The office needs fewer clerks. After some training, Ines and one other clerk moved to the help desk, where they help people with hard problems. The third clerk lost her work.

cases.name: Teacher at the learning centre
cases.body: Ms Rana uses an AI tool to make practice questions. She checks every question, because the tool sometimes makes mistakes. She now has more time to help learners one by one.

cases.name: Tailor at the market
cases.body: Sami makes and mends clothes. A translation tool helps him talk with customers who speak other languages, so he has more customers. The tool can't sew, and it can't measure a person.

sections.heading: New machines have changed work before
sections.text: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in cloth factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as Luddites, broke machines in protest, because the machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. Instead, a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That was one machine in one country, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
sections.simpler: AI is not the first technology to change work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Some workers, called Luddites, broke machines in protest. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got cash machines. Many thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. But a 2015 study found there were still about as many. Banks opened more branches. The workers counted less cash and helped customers more. That was one machine in one country. It can't tell us what AI will do.

sections.heading: AI changes tasks inside jobs
sections.text: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work, but the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, studied AI tools that write and make things. Its researchers scored about 30,000 tasks for how much of each one these tools could do. They found that about one in four of the world's jobs has some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type in data, have the most. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. It is not a count of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.
sections.simpler: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group for work studied AI that writes and makes things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About one in four jobs has some exposure to these tools. That means the tools could do some of the tasks. Office jobs have the most. This is not a count of lost jobs. Most of these jobs will likely change, not disappear.

sections.heading: The change is uneven
sections.text: The same change can affect people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, against about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's are in the most exposed group. Change can be uneven inside one office too. In the made-up town of Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third lost her work. The ILO says talks between workers, employers and governments can help to manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
sections.simpler: Change can affect people in different ways. The ILO found more exposure in richer countries. There, about one in three jobs has some. In the poorest countries, it is about one in ten. In richer countries, more women's jobs than men's are very exposed. In made-up Millbrook, the water office works faster now. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. Workers, employers and leaders can plan these changes together, the ILO says.

glossary.definition: Tools and machines that people make to solve problems.
glossary.example: Cash machines were a new technology in banks.

glossary.definition: To make a machine do work that people used to do.
glossary.example: The water office used AI to automate reading forms.

glossary.definition: One piece of work that is part of a job.
glossary.example: Typing up forms was one task for the Millbrook clerks.

glossary.definition: When a new tool could do some of the tasks in a job.
glossary.example: Office jobs have the most exposure to AI tools that write.

glossary.definition: Lessons that teach people the skills for new work.
glossary.example: After training, two Millbrook clerks moved to the help desk.

glossary.definition: A person or company that pays people to work for them.
glossary.example: The water office is the clerks' employer.

checks.question: What happened to bank tellers in the United States as cash machines spread?

options.text: Their work changed to helping customers
options.feedback: Yes. A 2015 study found about as many tellers, and they spent more time helping customers.

options.text: All of the tellers lost their work
options.feedback: Not quite. Many people expected this, but it didn't happen. Read the end of the first section.

options.text: Tellers began to build cash machines
options.feedback: Not quite. Tellers still worked in banks. Read what they spent more time doing.

checks.question: When the ILO says a job has some exposure to AI tools, what does it mean?

options.text: The job has already been lost
options.feedback: Not quite. Exposure is not a count of lost jobs. Read the second section.

options.text: The worker uses a computer every day
options.feedback: Not quite. Exposure is about the tasks in the job. Read the second section.

options.text: The tools could do some of its tasks
options.feedback: Yes. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. Most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear.

write.prompt: Choose one Millbrook worker. Explain which of their tasks changed, and who gained or lost. Then say how it is like or unlike one change from history in the lesson.
write.example: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. The task that changed was typing up forms, because an AI tool now reads most of them. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work moved towards helping people. It is also unlike them, because one clerk lost her job, while the number of tellers did not fall.

speak.partnerTask: Talk with your partner: what could the Millbrook water office have done so that the third clerk kept her work? Each give one idea, and say who would need to agree to it.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud what the ILO means by exposure, and why it is not the same as losing a job.

watch.title: The big debate about the future of work, explained
watch.why: It looks back at a hundred years of worry about machines taking jobs, and asks who gains from new technology.
watch.beforeQuestion: Do you think new machines make more jobs or fewer jobs? Why?
watch.afterQuestion: Why does the video say that who gains from technology depends on people's choices?
watch.summary: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
keyPoints: People have worried about machines taking jobs many times before.
New technology removes some jobs but also helps create new ones.
Who gains from technology depends on the rules and choices people make.
watch.contentNote: Vox, 2017: made before today's AI chat tools, and about the United States. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed (October 2026); the length, about 9 minutes, comes from Rosetta's transcript archive and is not confirmed on YouTube. It mentions IBM's Watson, a 2013 Oxford study and US income figures. The summary was written from that archive's transcript summary, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

sources.label: The Conversable Economist (2015): ATMs and a rising number of bank tellers? (on James Bessen's research in the IMF's Finance & Development)
International Labour Organization (20 May 2025): Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (research brief; potential exposure of tasks, not job losses)
ILO Working Paper 140 (2025): Generative AI and jobs, a refined global index of occupational exposure (Gmyrek and others; figures by country income group and by sex)

sensitiveNotes: Many learners may not be allowed to work where they live, and work and money can be painful topics for families. Never ask learners about their own or their family's jobs, income or plans for work. The lesson uses made-up Millbrook workers, and the Speak discussion is about them.
Britannica notes that the government punished the Luddites harshly, including hangings. The lesson leaves this out; if learners ask, keep it short and factual.
educatorNotes: One estimate in learner text, on purpose: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek and others, 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK; ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks for how far generative AI could do them. 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations with some exposure (34% in high-income countries, 11% in low-income ones); 3.3% are in the most exposed group, mostly clerical jobs such as data entry clerks and typists; in high-income countries that group is 9.6% of women's jobs and 3.5% of men's. The ILO says the figures reflect potential exposure, an upper limit, not the actual effect on employment; it expects most jobs to be transformed rather than made redundant, though efficiency gains could still reduce demand for workers. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: almost 40% of jobs exposed to AI in general), cover a wider set of technologies and use another method, so they can't be set beside the ILO's number; the lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015), and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015); each is one past case, not a forecast for AI.

The Speak discussion has no single right answer. Ideas might include retraining the clerk for another task, moving more slowly, or sharing the remaining work; ask who would have to agree (the employer, the workers, a union or the government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between them. A teacher could add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's own job.

Social studies angle with history: cloth machines and the Luddites (1811–1816), cash machines and bank tellers, spreadsheets and bookkeepers, then the ILO's 2025 and the IMF's 2024 findings on AI and jobs, and who gains or loses.
